showpieces.name: Make a wallet
showpieces.does: Generate a key pair and a seed phrase in the browser, see how the address is derived, then sign and verify a message.

showpieces.name: Send a transaction and watch it
showpieces.does: Build, sign and broadcast a transfer, then watch it move through the RPC and open it in NearBlocks. Uses a practice account the app funds from a testnet faucet.

showpieces.name: Why moving money between chains is hard
showpieces.does: Two chains, one coin. Try to move it and see where trust or delay comes in. Sets up Stage 4.

showpieces.name: Claim your name
showpieces.does: Pick a name and create your own testnet account, then compare it with a plain hex account.

showpieces.name: A key that can do only one thing
showpieces.does: Add a function-call key limited to one contract and a small allowance, hand it to an AI agent, then try to trick the agent into overspending or calling something else. The chain refuses every attempt. Delete the key to finish.

showpieces.name: Inside a NEAR transaction
showpieces.does: Bundle several actions (create a sub-account, send NEAR, add a key) into one transaction and see them succeed or fail together.

showpieces.name: Follow your transaction across shards
showpieces.does: 3D showpiece. Pick your own earlier transaction and see which shard handled it, which chunk and block it landed in, and how fast it finalised.

showpieces.name: A call that takes several blocks
showpieces.does: Make a cross-contract call and watch its receipts hop between blocks and shards, with the gas burned and the 30% paid to the contract.

showpieces.name: Stateless validation, resharding and staking
showpieces.does: Animated explainer of how a validator checks a shard without its state and how shards split. Includes staking testnet NEAR and seeing the unstake delay.

showpieces.name: Deploy a contract in one click
showpieces.does: Deploy a ready-made contract to your own sub-account, call it, read its state, and trigger a callback and a failure.

showpieces.name: Issue your own token
showpieces.does: Create a fungible token, send it gaslessly through a relayer, and see the storage registration NEAR requires.

showpieces.name: Race the RPC nodes
showpieces.does: Send the same query to several providers, compare speed, kill one and watch failover. Shows why wallets don't trust a single node.

showpieces.name: One account, every chain
showpieces.does: 3D showpiece. Derive an Ethereum address from your NEAR account, then sign and send a Sepolia transaction through the signing network.

showpieces.name: Swap across chains with an intent
showpieces.does: Request a live quote for a cross-chain swap, see the solvers compete, and optionally run a tiny real swap.

showpieces.name: Old bridge vs the NEAR way
showpieces.does: Side-by-side steps, time, fees and trust for a classic bridge and an intent, using live quote data. Ends with the private-swap option.

showpieces.name: Ask a private AI and verify it
showpieces.does: Chat with the tutor running on NEAR AI Cloud, then fetch the attestation and check the enclave and response signature yourself.

showpieces.name: An agent with no owner
showpieces.does: Animated walk-through of an agent inside a TEE that controls a multichain account, plus a read-only look at a deployed agent.

showpieces.name: Read and vote on a proposal
showpieces.does: Browse live governance proposals and see how locked tokens turn into voting power. Voting is optional.

showpieces.name: The live money map
showpieces.does: Live view of intents volume, stablecoins and major DeFi apps, with notes on oracles and launchpads.

showpieces.name: Trace one intent end to end
showpieces.does: Capstone. Follow a single cross-chain intent through accounts, keys, shards, receipts and signatures, then take the final exam and mint the Book of NEAR badge.

showpieces.name: The honest scoreboard
showpieces.does: Weigh NEAR against Ethereum, Solana and Cosmos on the things you care about, with the real weak spots shown.

topics.name: Money, ledgers and why blockchains exist
topics.comparison: Universal concept; teach once, chain-agnostic.

topics.name: Hashing and blocks
topics.comparison: Same on every chain.

topics.name: Public/private keys and signatures
topics.comparison: Standard. NEAR mainly uses ed25519 keys and also supports secp256k1; Ethereum and Bitcoin use secp256k1, Solana ed25519.

topics.name: What a crypto wallet is and how it works
topics.comparison: Universal: a wallet holds keys and signs, the coins live on the chain. On NEAR the wallet also manages several access keys per account.

topics.name: Wallet creation: private key, public key, address
topics.comparison: Bitcoin and Ethereum addresses are hashes of the public key. A NEAR implicit account is the hex of the ed25519 public key itself, and a named account (alice.near) separates the address from any key completely.

topics.name: Key standards: secp256k1, ed25519, BIP-39, BIP-32/44, SLIP-10
topics.comparison: Standard cryptography. NEAR wallets use BIP-39 seed phrases with SLIP-10 ed25519 derivation on path m/44'/397'/0' (397 is NEAR's coin type). Ethereum uses secp256k1 with BIP-32 on m/44'/60'/0'/0/0.

topics.name: Self-custody, seed phrase safety and scams
topics.comparison: Standard; the scam-safety part matters more than anything chain-specific.

topics.name: How wallets interact with blockchains
topics.comparison: Universal pattern: the wallet reads state and sends signed transactions through an RPC node, and connects to apps through a connector (WalletConnect on Ethereum, NEAR Connect on NEAR).

topics.name: What RPCs are and how they work (JSON-RPC)
topics.comparison: Same idea everywhere: an HTTP endpoint on a node that answers queries and accepts transactions. NEAR's methods (query, block, chunk, send_tx, tx) differ in names only.

topics.name: Transaction lifecycle: construct, sign, broadcast, confirm
topics.comparison: Universal steps. The NEAR-specific anatomy comes in Stage 1.

topics.name: Consensus 101: proof of work vs proof of stake
topics.summary: A blockchain needs rules for who adds the next block. Proof of work picks the winner by spent computing power; proof of stake picks by coins locked up as a deposit.
topics.comparison: NEAR is proof of stake, like Ethereum, Solana and Cosmos chains.

topics.name: Transactions, fees and gas
topics.comparison: Standard idea. NEAR's fees are tiny and predictable compared with Ethereum L1.

topics.name: Smart contracts
topics.summary: A smart contract is a program stored on a blockchain. Anyone can call it, and it runs the same way for everyone who checks it.
topics.comparison: Standard concept.

topics.name: Tokens: fungible, NFTs, stablecoins
topics.summary: Tokens are assets that live on a chain. Fungible tokens are all alike, NFTs are one of a kind, and stablecoins aim to keep the value of a currency such as the dollar.
topics.comparison: Standard concept.

topics.name: Reading a block explorer
topics.comparison: Same skill everywhere (Etherscan, Solscan, NearBlocks).

topics.name: DEXs, AMMs and liquidity
topics.summary: A DEX (decentralised exchange) is a contract that swaps tokens with no company in the middle. Most trade against pools of tokens that people deposit, called liquidity.
topics.comparison: Standard DeFi concept.

topics.name: Layer 1, layer 2, bridges and why cross-chain is hard
topics.summary: A layer 1 is a base chain; a layer 2 runs on top of one. Moving value between chains needs a bridge, and every bridge adds some trust or some waiting.
topics.comparison: Needed as the 'before' picture for NEAR Intents and Chain Signatures.

topics.name: Named accounts and sub-accounts (alice.near)
topics.comparison: On Ethereum the account is a 0x hash and ENS is a naming layer on top. On NEAR the readable name is the account itself, and owners create sub-accounts. EOS also had native named accounts.

topics.name: Implicit accounts (64-hex) and Ethereum-style 0x accounts
topics.comparison: Implicit accounts work like Ethereum addresses derived from a key. 0x 'ETH-implicit' accounts let an Ethereum wallet control a NEAR account through a wallet contract.

topics.name: Access keys: full-access vs function-call keys
topics.comparison: Ethereum and Solana accounts have one key with full power; scoped keys there need smart wallets (ERC-4337). NEAR has many keys per account natively, including keys limited to one contract and an allowance. This is what makes 'log in without popups' work.

topics.name: NEAR transaction anatomy: signer, receiver, actions, nonce, block hash
topics.comparison: One NEAR transaction carries a list of actions (create account, add key, deploy, call, transfer) that run together. The nonce belongs to the access key, not the account, and the transaction must cite a recent block hash so it expires after about a day. An Ethereum transaction is one call with an account-wide nonce.

topics.name: How NEAR apps connect to wallets (NEAR Connect, key-based login, NEP-413)
topics.comparison: Apps request a function-call key at login, so small actions need no wallet popup. Ethereum apps ask the wallet to sign every transaction. Apps can also ask for a signed message (NEP-413), like Sign-In with Ethereum (EIP-4361).

topics.name: NEAR token, yoctoNEAR units and supply
topics.comparison: Standard native token. 1 NEAR = 10^24 yocto.

topics.name: Storage staking
topics.comparison: Data stored on chain locks NEAR (1 NEAR per 100 KB) and is refunded when deleted. Solana's rent-exempt balance is similar. Ethereum charges once and stores forever.

topics.name: Wallets: Meteor, HOT, MyNearWallet, Intear, Ledger, passkey and email sign-in
topics.comparison: Standard wallet landscape. HOT Wallet drives most NEAR transactions (about 65% in Q2 2026 per Nansen). Passkey and email onboarding compares with Privy, Web3Auth and Coinbase Smart Wallet; NEAR's FastAuth was an earlier version.

topics.name: Sharding: Nightshade (one chain, chunks per shard)
topics.comparison: Ethereum dropped execution sharding in favour of rollups; Solana runs one global state; Polkadot and Cosmos use separate chains. NEAR splits one chain into shards, each block carrying a 'chunk' per shard, invisible to users.

topics.name: Stateless validation (Nightshade 2.0)
topics.summary: Validators check a shard's work without keeping all of that shard's data. They check a small bundle of evidence that travels with each chunk instead.
topics.comparison: Chunk validators check a 'state witness' without storing full state. Ethereum has researched statelessness (Verkle trees) but hasn't shipped it on L1. Live on NEAR mainnet since 2024.

topics.name: Dynamic resharding
topics.summary: Resharding changes how accounts are spread across shards. It lets the network make room as use grows.
topics.comparison: Shards split or merge by load without governance votes (network upgrade 2.13, 2026). Mainnet went from 6 to 9 shards in late 2025. No major L1 resizes shards automatically.

topics.name: Doomslug block production and finality
topics.comparison: About 600 ms blocks and about 1.2 s finality. Solana has ~400 ms slots but slower full finality; Ethereum 12 s slots and ~13 min finality; CometBFT chains finalise in seconds.

topics.name: Validators, epochs and staking (pools, liquid staking)
topics.summary: Validators are the computers that make and check blocks. People lock up NEAR with them (staking) to help secure the network and earn rewards.
topics.comparison: Proof-of-stake basics with NEAR-specific roles (block producers, chunk producers, chunk validators) and roughly 12-hour epochs. Liquid staking tokens (stNEAR, LiNEAR, rNEAR) work like Lido on Ethereum.

topics.name: Receipts and asynchronous execution
topics.comparison: On Ethereum and Solana, contract-to-contract calls are synchronous and atomic in one transaction. On NEAR they become receipts that can execute in later blocks on other shards, so a 'transaction' can partially succeed. Cosmos IBC is async too, but between chains.

topics.name: Gas economics: 30% of fees go to the contract
topics.comparison: Ethereum burns the base fee and gives contracts nothing. NEAR burns 70% and pays 30% to the called contract, a built-in developer revenue stream.

topics.name: How NEAR is governed and paid: validator-vote upgrades and tokenomics
topics.summary: How the protocol changes and who gets paid. Validators upgrade their software, and new NEAR is issued as rewards for securing the network.
topics.comparison: Upgrades activate once 80% of stake runs them, with no chain split, similar to Tezos or Cosmos governance upgrades while Ethereum coordinates hard forks. Issuance is standard proof of stake: validators voted the maximum inflation from 5% to 2.5% with protocol version 81 (Oct 2025).

topics.name: Roadmap: SPICE (consensus separated from execution)
topics.summary: A planned change that separates agreeing on the order of blocks from running what is in them. The aim is faster blocks.
topics.comparison: Aims for ~200 ms blocks. Monad, Sui and Aptos already decouple execution, so the idea isn't new; doing it on a sharded chain is.

topics.name: Post-quantum keys (ML-DSA) and key rotation
topics.summary: Future quantum computers could break today's signatures. Because NEAR accounts can swap their keys, moving to new quantum-safe keys could be easier.
topics.comparison: Because accounts can rotate keys, they can move to quantum-safe keys without changing address. Ethereum externally owned accounts cannot rotate keys.

topics.name: Contracts in WebAssembly (Rust, JS/TS) and near-sdk
topics.comparison: Ethereum uses the EVM and Solidity; Solana compiles Rust to its own VM. Cosmos CosmWasm also uses Wasm.

topics.name: Cross-contract calls, promises and callbacks
topics.comparison: Follows from async receipts: you must handle callbacks and failures yourself. Very different from Solidity's synchronous calls.

topics.name: Contract state, storage management (NEP-145), upgrades and global contracts
topics.comparison: Upgrading means redeploying code to the same account, so no proxy pattern like Ethereum's. Storage must be registered or paid for. Global contracts let many accounts reuse one deployed code, cutting storage for factories; Ethereum uses minimal proxies (EIP-1167).

topics.name: Token standards: NEP-141, NEP-171, NEP-245, NEP-297 events
topics.comparison: Roughly ERC-20, ERC-721, ERC-1155. NEP-141 uses ft_transfer_call instead of approve plus transferFrom, and needs storage registration.

topics.name: Meta-transactions and relayers (NEP-366)
topics.comparison: Gasless transactions are built into the protocol. Ethereum needs ERC-4337 bundlers and paymasters.

topics.name: RPC providers vs running your own node
topics.comparison: Same trade-off on every chain: providers (FastNEAR, Lava, Ankr and others) are easy but you trust and depend on them; your own nearcore node costs hardware and upkeep. NEAR specifics: regular vs archival nodes, and the free public endpoint is rate-limited, so production apps use providers with failover.

topics.name: Data infrastructure: NEAR Lake, indexers, explorer APIs
topics.comparison: Comparable to Ethereum's indexing stack (The Graph, Etherscan API).

topics.name: Building a public non-custodial wallet: architecture
topics.summary: What it takes to build a wallet that never holds its users' keys. Key storage, signing, talking to RPC nodes and guarding users against phishing.
topics.comparison: Common parts: key generation and encrypted storage (or passkeys/MPC), signing, RPC with failover, Ledger support, phishing protection. Extra on NEAR: creating named accounts (needs a funded creator or relayer), managing several access keys and their allowances, NEP-413 message signing, NEAR Connect integration, and Chain Signatures for other chains.

topics.name: Aurora (EVM on NEAR)
topics.summary: Aurora runs Ethereum's virtual machine (the EVM) on NEAR. Apps written for Ethereum can run there with few changes.
topics.comparison: An EVM running as a NEAR contract, so Solidity apps can deploy. Compare with EVM layers on Cosmos (Evmos) or Polkadot (Moonbeam).

topics.name: Chain Signatures (MPC signing for other chains)
topics.comparison: A NEAR account or contract controls addresses on Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and more, signed by a decentralised MPC network. Nearest equivalents: ICP's threshold ECDSA, Lit Protocol, ZetaChain TSS. The lesson also shows how a contract pauses and resumes (yield and resume, NEP-519) while the network signs.

topics.name: NEAR Intents (verifier, solvers, 1Click)
topics.comparison: Intent-based trading exists elsewhere (UniswapX, CoW Swap, Across). NEAR's version is a cross-chain settlement layer across 35+ chains, with over $22B cumulative volume.

topics.name: Omni Bridge (successor to Rainbow Bridge)
topics.comparison: Combines light clients with Chain Signatures. Compare Wormhole, LayerZero, Axelar.

topics.name: Confidential Intents (private shard plus TEE bridge)
topics.comparison: Private swaps exist (Railgun, Aztec, Penumbra). NEAR's runs on a permissioned private shard bridged by trusted hardware, so you trust TEEs and those validators. About 42% of near.com swap volume is private by default.

topics.name: Multichain accounts: one NEAR account, many chains
topics.comparison: Built on Chain Signatures. Smart-wallet projects on other chains aim at the same UX but usually need a bridge or custody.

topics.name: TEEs and remote attestation basics
topics.summary: A TEE (trusted execution environment) is a sealed area inside a chip. Code runs there out of reach of the machine's owner, and the chip can prove which code runs (remote attestation).
topics.comparison: General hardware technology (Intel TDX, NVIDIA confidential GPUs), not NEAR-specific. Prerequisite for the three topics after it.

topics.name: NEAR AI Cloud: confidential inference and stake-to-compute
topics.summary: A service that runs AI models inside TEEs, so prompts stay private. You can check the hardware's proof yourself.
topics.comparison: Models run inside Intel TDX plus H200 GPU enclaves with attestation you can verify yourself; OpenAI-compatible API. You can also stake NEAR to earn inference credits instead of paying per call. Compare Phala, Secret AI, Apple Private Cloud Compute (closed).

topics.name: Shade Agents (TEE agents holding multichain keys)
topics.summary: Programs that run inside a TEE and control accounts on many chains. No person holds their keys.
topics.comparison: Agents run in a TEE and control Chain Signature accounts, so no human holds the key. Compare Phala agents and Autonolas.

topics.name: User-owned AI and agents on NEAR
topics.summary: The idea that people, not platforms, should own their AI agents and data. This topic shows which NEAR pieces are built for that.
topics.comparison: The NEAR AI vision. Many chains pitch AI agents; the private-inference and Chain Signatures pieces are the concrete differences.

topics.name: House of Stake, veNEAR and DAOs
topics.summary: How NEAR holders take part in decisions. Locking NEAR gives voting power, and DAOs let groups run shared funds by vote.
topics.comparison: Vote-escrow model borrowed from Curve (veCRV). Small validators and veNEAR holders got extra rewards in the 2025 tokenomics change. DAOs (Sputnik, AstroDAO) compare with Snapshot plus Safe on Ethereum and get a short mention here.

topics.name: DeFi map and market glossary: Rhea (Ref), lending, stablecoins, oracles, launchpads
topics.summary: A tour of the money apps on NEAR: exchanges, lending, stablecoins and price feeds (oracles). It explains the words you will meet.
topics.comparison: Standard DeFi building blocks; native USDC and USDT exist on NEAR. Oracles (Pyth) are the same ones used across chains. Launchpads and memecoin factories follow the pump.fun pattern on Solana. Oracles and launchpads get a short mention here, with no lesson of their own.

topics.name: Capstone: trace a cross-chain intent end to end
topics.comparison: Ties together accounts, keys, receipts, shards, Chain Signatures and Intents in one real transaction.

topics.name: Capstone: the honest take
topics.summary: Where NEAR is strong and where it is weak, next to other chains. It gathers the honest takes from every lesson into one scoreboard.
topics.comparison: NEAR's strengths and weaknesses (async complexity, TEE trust, ecosystem size, HOT concentration) versus competitors.
